ATP
AY-tee-PEE (or spoken in full)
abbreviation (Gen-Z slang)
Text abbreviation of at this point, used to signal that a situation has gone on so long, or so badly, that the speaker has reached a conclusion — usually an exasperated one ("atp just cancel the game"). The initialism spread on Twitter and TikTok c. 2019–2021. It collides with older initialisms: biology students know ATP as adenosine triphosphate, and sports fans know it as the men’s professional tennis tour.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang atp marks a verdict reached after too much: "atp I’m just going to fail this class," "atp she’s not even trying." It is the sound of someone giving up with a shrug, sometimes funny, sometimes bitter. The Christian observation: the letters are harmless; the mood they often carry is not small. "At this point" is the voice of weariness deciding that what has been is what will be. Scripture speaks to that voice directly. "Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not" (Gal 6:9). Jeremiah wrote Lamentations from the rubble of Jerusalem, at the lowest point a man could reach, and still confessed that the LORD’s "compassions fail not" (Lam 3:22): "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lam 3:23). Paul, pressed on every side, could write that he was "perplexed, but not in despair" (2Co 4:8). The believer’s "at this point" is never the last point, because God has not finished. "They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles" (Isa 40:31). There is a right kind of conclusion — changing a plan that is plainly not working is often wisdom — and a wrong kind, which is deciding that God’s promises have run out. A father tells his son: you may be tired, and you may need to change course, but never let a hard week write the verdict on your life; at this point, and at every point, the Lord is still at work.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z text-speak (c. 2019–present) for "at this point," marking an exasperated conclusion — harmless in itself, though it often voices a weariness Scripture meets with mercies new every morning.

expand to see more

ATP, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2019–present; Twitter, TikTok, texting) "At this point"; signals a conclusion reached after too much of something. "Atp I’m just going to sleep in the car."

Often begins a resigned or sarcastic verdict: "atp he should just apologize," "atp it’s embarrassing."

Older senses a grandparent will know: in biology, ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the molecule that carries energy in living cells; in sport, the Association of Tennis Professionals.

Webster (1828), root word point: “POINT, noun [&hellip;] 1. The sharp end of any instrument or body; as the point of a knife, of a sword or of a thorn. 2. A string with a tag; as a silken point 3. A small cape, headland or promontory; a tract of land extending into the sea, a lake or river, beyond the line of the shore, and becoming narrow at the end; as point Judith;”

Decode for parents: a harmless abbreviation; listen for whether it is a joke or a child quietly giving up.

Key Scripture

Gal 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Lam 3:22 — "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."

Lam 3:23 — "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

2Co 4:8 — "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;"

Isa 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Modern Corruption

ATP is a neutral abbreviation that often carries resignation — weariness deciding the future from the past — which Scripture answers with God’s faithfulness in due season.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong with the letters. Sometimes "at this point" is plain good sense: the bus is not coming, call home. But the phrase is often the way a young person narrates surrender — to a class, a friendship, a sin he has stopped fighting. "Atp I’m just like this." The world encourages that shrug and calls it accepting yourself. Scripture calls it fainting, and warns against it, because the harvest comes "in due season" only to those who "faint not" (Gal 6:9).

The cure is not a pep talk but a Person. Lamentations is the Bible’s book of "at this point" — city burned, temple gone, the poet sitting in the ashes — and at its centre stands the confession that God’s compassions "are new every morning" (Lam 3:23). Paul could be "perplexed, but not in despair" (2Co 4:8) because his hope did not rest on how the week had gone. Teach your children the difference between changing course, which is often wisdom, and giving up on God’s promises, which never is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin punctum (a prick, a dot) → English point → "at this point" (at this stage) → atp online c. 2019–2021.

expand to see more

Latin punctum, from pungo, to prick — a dot, a mark

English point — a place or a moment in a process

"At this point" — at this stage of affairs; often impatient

c. 2019–2021 Twitter and TikTok: atp as a resigned or sarcastic verdict
